claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is governed by interfacial misfit stress fields.
Interfacial misfit stress fields pin dislocations at chemically and structurally distinct interfaces.
The alternating layers possess compositional differences.
The alternating layers possess lattice-parameter differences.
Reducing layer thickness increases interface density when total coating thickness is held constant.
Keeping the deposition method constant makes interface characteristics the only relevant variable.
Lattice mismatch at multilayer interfaces creates localized misfit stress fields.
Compositional gradients at multilayer interfaces create localized misfit stress fields.
The localized interfacial stress fields act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Chemically complex and structurally distinct interfaces generate internal stress fields.
The interface-generated internal stress fields hinder dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation glide reduces the accumulation and propagation of plastic deformation under sustained loads.
Multilayer coatings with higher interface density and thinner layers will exhibit slower time-dependent plastic deformation.
Higher-interface-density multilayers will have lower creep strain rates than homogeneous coatings of the same overall composition and thickness.
Higher-interface-density multilayers will retain hardness better than homogeneous coatings of the same overall composition and thickness.
The proposed mechanism applies when thermal diffusion does not significantly alter the interface structures.
The proposed mechanism applies only at stress levels that do not override dislocation pinning.
Extremely high temperatures or stresses may activate additional deformation mechanisms not included in the hypothesis.
The relative contributions of interfacial misfit and chemical complexity may vary with alloy system and layer design.
